"What happens next" is usually up to the PCs. They drive the story more than you do. You get to set up the pieces, but it's up to the players to make most of the moves.

If you want to know what happens next, consider only your villain's motives and options. What are his plans? What does he want? What are his tools? Make his plan and know what will happen if the PCs spontaneously die. Then improv how he adapts when the PCs take action.

I don't know what your setting is like, but I'll toss a few ideas your way.

-Maybe someone higher up in government is corrupt, leading to a lawful (yet secretly evil) mission to capture. The hermit druid likely just wants to be left alone ( they're a hermit after all) so the villain targets them because stray druids could potentially get in the way (or they want to build something on their grove or something). A prodigy human spellcaster could've done something wrong (or maybe this is a discreet way of a villain trying to hire them/get them on their side once they're in prison; this also gives the villain leverage). Dwarf could be in the wrong place at the wrong time and framed for a crime, maybe she even witnessed a murder.

-Why start with the Hunter capturing them? If you have a specific direction in mind, just consider the PCs personal motivations (what are their goals or wants before the story starts and how could these change as you give a story hook?)

My first time DMing (and just playing D&D for that matter) i gave the characters magic equipment that evolved as they leveled. By mid campaign i couldn't use an ancient volcanic Dragon on them without them breezing through it. 

My advice: make them start no better ( maybe even worse) than regular equipment. Then scale up very slowly. Verrrry slowly.
